paras: The mob attack on Daniel Lewis took place in July 1903 near Ninety-fourth Street and First Avenue in New York City, when a crowd of men chased Lewis, a Black man, shouted "Lynch him!" and, by one account, beat him after an encounter with two girls carrying ice. Police took him from the crowd, and a magistrate sent him to Bellevue to be examined as to his sanity. Outside New York the incident circulated as a single paragraph in wire reports of a deadly heat wave, under headlines saying he had narrowly escaped lynching.

The episode occurred during a heat wave that the wire reports said had caused thirty-eight deaths in and around New York and Brooklyn on July 10, the hottest July 10 in the local weather bureau's records. Lewis lived at 234 East Ninety-eighth Street, and his mother later told the court that he had been acting "queerly" for some days.

Dora Stida, fourteen, and her twelve-year-old sister Annie had fetched a piece of ice from the ice pier at East Ninety-first Street and were carrying it in a tin pan, according to the Tribune; the Sun has them dragging it on a little wagon. According to the New-York Tribune, Lewis sprang toward them near Ninety-fourth Street, demanded the ice and lifted a club, and three men ran up and knocked him down before he could strike. A cry then went up that "a negro had attempted to assault two little girls," men came from all directions, and the crowd was beating him and shouting "Lynch him!" when detectives of the East Eighty-eighth Street station reached and arrested him.

The Sun, drawing on the story told in court, said instead that Lewis had gone "mad from the heat," ran down First Avenue and made a dash for the ice, and that the girls ran while men in the street, thinking he had attacked them, chased him. In its account it took three policemen to catch Lewis and "explain things to the crowd."

Lewis was arraigned in the Harlem police court on a charge of disorderly conduct and sent to Bellevue for examination as to his sanity, by Magistrate Baker according to the Tribune and by Magistrate Breen according to the Sun. No arrest of anyone in the crowd is reported, and the coverage does not show the result of the sanity examination.

The two New York papers framed the same hearing differently: the Tribune headlined "Wanted to Lynch Negro" and "Crowd Was Beating Him When Detectives Arrived," while opening with the attempted assault as fact. The Sun's headline, "Chase for Heat-Crazed Negro," was followed by "Crowd Thought He'd Attacked Two Little Girls—What He Wanted Was Ice," presenting the attack as the crowd's mistake.

The wire version, datelined New York, July 10, adopted the attack without qualification, describing "a heat-crazed negro" who "attacked with a club two girls," and placed it among reports of deaths and prostrations from the heat. It ran on July 11 in papers in Kansas, Nebraska, Oregon, Virginia and Arizona, with the Omaha Daily Bee dropping the words "heat-crazed." Some editors raised the item into their subheads, which said Lewis "Narrowly Escaped Lynching" or "Might Have Been Lynched but for Detectives."

The paragraph appeared in the Raleigh News & Observer on July 12, the Atlanta Constitution on July 13 and weekly papers such as the Kinsley Graphic as late as July 17. No coverage of the incident in the Black press was found.

The accounts disagree on whether Lewis attacked the girls: the Tribune and the wire say he did or tried to with a club, while the Sun says he only went for their ice and the crowd mistook his intent. Only the Tribune reports that the crowd beat him, and the papers also differ on the date, with the Sun placing it on Thursday night, July 9, and the Tribune on Friday afternoon, July 10.

reader.title: Mob attack on Daniel Lewis
bases: A street crowd chased Lewis, shouted 'Lynch him!' and, by the Tribune's account, knocked him down and beat him before detectives or policemen took him away; no one was killed (A1, A2, A3).

Lewis survived: he was rescued by detectives (or three policemen) and sent to Bellevue (A1, A2, A3). The crowd acted without authority on the belief that he had assaulted two girls, but no killing occurred, so this was at most a threatened lynching.

Two independent New York reports (A1, A2) and the wire paragraph (A3) agree that a crowd chased Lewis after an encounter with two girls carrying ice and that police took him away and sent him to a hospital, though they disagree on whether he attacked the girls and whether he was beaten.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune (local)
accounts.gist: Lewis allegedly sprang toward the girls, demanded the ice and raised a club; three men knocked him down, a cry went up that a negro had tried to assault two girls, and the crowd was beating him when detectives arrived.

accounts.label: The Sun (local, from the court hearing)
accounts.gist: Lewis, mad from the heat, dashed for the girls' ice; the men in the street mistakenly thought he had attacked them and chased him until three policemen caught him and explained things to the crowd.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A heat-crazed negro attacked two girls carrying ice with a club; a mob shouted 'Lynch him!' and detectives rescued him and sent him to a hospital.

The Sun headlined 'Chase for Heat-Crazed Negro' and 'Crowd Thought He'd Attacked Two Little Girls—What He Wanted Was Ice', presenting the attack as the crowd's mistake.
Papers from Oregon to Georgia ran the wire paragraph inside heat-wave stories, some adding subheads that he 'narrowly escaped lynching' or 'might have been lynched but for detectives'.

info: Thursday night, July 9, 1903, per the Sun; 'yesterday afternoon' (Friday, July 10) per the Tribune; the wire places it in its July 10 story
